title: Men like trees (Mark 8:22–26)
hook: the only two-stage healing: first blurry, then clear

segments.voice: Yesterday, hard hearts in a boat: one loaf, two feedings forgotten, and a string of questions. Your line was do you not yet understand? What did you remember? Day one hundred ninety-two.

If you've ever worn glasses, you know the moment at the eye doctor. They click through the lenses. Better like this? Or like this? The chart goes from smudge, to almost, to sharp. Today's healing happens exactly like that, and it's the only one in the Gospels that does. At Bethsaida, on the north shore of the lake, people bring a blind man to Jesus. And for the first and only time, the healing comes in two stages. Mark tells us what the man saw halfway through. Today: men like trees.
screen: `BETTER LIKE THIS, OR THIS?` → `BETHSAIDA.` → `THE FIRST TRY, HALFWAY.`

segments.voice: Jesus takes the man by the hand and leads him out of the village. Picture that walk: a blind man holding a stranger's hand down a dirt road. Then Jesus spits on his eyes, lays his hands on him, and asks, do you see anything? In the old King James Bible, the man looks up and says, "I see men as trees, walking." Blurry shapes, tall and moving. He can tell they're people only because trees don't walk. It's an honest answer. He doesn't pretend. So Jesus lays his hands on his eyes a second time, "and he was restored, and saw every man clearly." The word for clearly is a rare one, found only here in the New Testament. It means shining far off: he could see into the distance. Why would Mark tell a healing in two stages? Only Mark tells this one at all; Matthew and Luke leave it out. But look where Mark puts it. Just before, Jesus asked the disciples, having eyes, see ye not? Tomorrow, Peter will say who Jesus is, and then, in the very next breath, prove he only half understands it. Many readers think this blind man is a picture of the disciples. They see something. It's blurry. People look like trees. They'll need a second touch. Christians have long found comfort here. Faith doesn't always arrive in one flash. Healing often doesn't either. Sometimes you're honestly halfway, and the right answer to do you see? is, sort of. And the story says: that's not the end. There's a second touch.
screen: `LED BY THE HAND OUT OF TOWN.` · `I SEE MEN AS TREES, WALKING.` · `A SECOND TOUCH, THEN CLEARLY.` · `A PICTURE OF THE DISCIPLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with a slow change. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in you that's changing slowly. A habit you're breaking. A grief that's easing. A faith, or a doubt, that's taking shape. Ask it honestly, like Jesus asked the man: do you see anything yet? Maybe the answer is, sort of. Blurry. Men like trees. Let that be all right. If you pray, you can ask for the second touch. If not, just thank yourself for getting halfway. The bell holds the time.
Men like trees. What a blind man saw halfway through the only two-stage healing in the Gospels, before he saw clearly.
Your line: sight comes in stages. Today, be as patient with one slow change, in you or in someone else, as Jesus was with that man's eyes. Day one hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Many Christians describe faith as a journey rather than a single moment, and some churches pray for healing more than once, taking comfort from the second touch in this story.

original.note: Greek: clearly, shining far off. It appears only here in the New Testament.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle that took two tries.
what it means: an honest halfway answer, a second touch, and full sight: healing, and faith, can come in stages.
what a scholar hears: only Mark tells it, and he sets it between see ye not? and Peter's half-seeing confession, as a picture of the disciples.

notes: 'The only two-stage healing in the Gospels' and 'only Mark tells it' (no parallel in Matthew or Luke); confirm.
τηλαυγῶς as a New Testament hapax ('shining far off'); confirm.
Reading the blind man as a picture of the disciples (8:18 and 8:27–33) is a common interpretation attributed to 'many readers'.
Hook said the first try doesn't quite work; softened to the healing comes in two stages, since many Christians would not describe a healing by Jesus as a partial failure.
